questions.q: State Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity in your own words.
questions.a: Correct answer: When filling degenerate orbitals (same subshell), electrons occupy separate orbitals singly with parallel spins before any orbital gets a second electron. This maximizes total spin multiplicity. A wrong answer (e.g., "electrons pair up as soon as possible" or "electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy") reveals confusion with the Aufbau principle or a misunderstanding that pairing lowers energy. The student likely thinks electrons "prefer" to be paired, ignoring exchange energy and repulsion minimization.

questions.q: Why do electrons in degenerate orbitals prefer to remain unpaired with parallel spins rather than pair up in the same orbital? Explain using the concepts of electron-electron repulsion and exchange energy.
questions.a: Correct answer: Parallel spins in different orbitals keep electrons farther apart on average (reducing Coulombic repulsion) and allow quantum mechanical exchange interactions that lower the energy (exchange energy). Pairing forces two electrons into the same orbital, increasing repulsion and losing exchange stabilization. A wrong answer focusing only on Pauli exclusion ("opposite spins required in same orbital") misses the energetic driving force. The student may not grasp that Hund's rule is about energy minimization, not just a filling order.

questions.q: Draw the orbital diagram for the 3d subshell of a Fe²⁺ ion (Z=26). How many unpaired electrons does it have? Is Fe²⁺ paramagnetic or diamagnetic?
questions.a: Correct working: Fe atomic config = [Ar]4s²3d⁶. Fe²⁺ loses 4s² electrons → [Ar]3d⁶. For 3d⁶: five degenerate d orbitals. Hund's rule: first 5 electrons go singly into each orbital with parallel spins (↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑). The 6th electron pairs in one orbital (↑↓). Unpaired electrons = 4. Paramagnetic (attracted to magnetic field). A wrong answer (e.g., 2 unpaired or 0 unpaired) shows the student paired electrons too early (violating Hund's rule) or miscounted d orbitals. They may also incorrectly remove 3d electrons before 4s for the ion.

questions.q: Compare the orbital diagrams of nitrogen (1s²2s²2p³) and oxygen (1s²2s²2p⁴). Explain why nitrogen has a half-filled p subshell and how this affects its ionization energy relative to oxygen.
questions.a: Correct answer: Nitrogen (2p³): three electrons singly occupy all three p orbitals with parallel spins (↑ ↑ ↑) — half-filled, maximum exchange energy, symmetrical distribution, extra stable. Oxygen (2p⁴): one orbital has paired electrons (↑↓), two orbitals have single electrons (↑ ↑). The paired electrons in oxygen experience greater repulsion, making it easier to remove one (lower ionization energy) despite oxygen's higher nuclear charge. This explains the anomaly where IE(O) < IE(N). A wrong answer that doesn't mention exchange energy or symmetrical distribution fails to connect Hund's rule to the periodic trend anomaly.

questions.q: A student draws the orbital diagram for a 2p⁴ configuration as: Orbital 1: ↑, Orbital 2: ↑, Orbital 3: ↑, and places the fourth electron in a "fourth p orbital" (↑). Identify the error and draw the correct diagram.
questions.a: Error: A p subshell has exactly three orbitals (px, py, pz). There is no fourth p orbital. The fourth electron must pair in one of the three existing orbitals. Correct diagram: One orbital with ↑↓, two orbitals with ↑ each. All unpaired electrons have parallel spins. A wrong answer reveals the student doesn't know the number of orbitals per subshell (p=3, d=5, f=7) — a prerequisite from quantum numbers (ml values). They may also draw the paired electrons with parallel spins (violating Pauli).

questions.q: Give the correct order of steps for the magnet experiment that reveals unpaired d-electrons in three salt solutions.
questions.a: The procedure runs: (1) Fill identical tubes with FeSO4, CuSO4 and ZnSO4 solutions (2) Hang each from a strong magnet in turn and note attraction or not (3) Explain Fe2+ with d6 as four unpaired and Cu2+ with d9 as one unpaired (4) Confirm Zn2+ with d10 has no unpaired electrons and shows no pull. A wrong answer that expects zinc to be magnetic shows the student has misapplied Hund's rule, which fills d orbitals singly first and pairs only after each orbital has one electron.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Hund's Rule of Maximum ______ states that when electrons occupy degenerate orbitals (orbitals of equal energy within the same subshell), they occupy separate orbitals singly with parallel spins before any pairing occurs.
Fill in the blank: Observe a magnetic stirrer in the chemistry lab: the stir bar (iron) is strongly ______ to the rotating magnet beneath the beaker, while a ceramic stir bar is not.
Fill in the blank: How do four electrons arrange in three degenerate ______p orbitals?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can: (1) Draw correct orbital diagrams for any p, d, or f subshell applying Hund's rule, showing parallel spins for unpaired electrons; (2) Predict the number of unpaired electrons in atoms/ions and determine magnetic behavior (paramagnetic/diamagnetic); (3) Explain the extra stability of half-filled and fully-filled subshells.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Observe a magnetic stirrer in the ______ lab: the stir bar (iron) is strongly attracted to the rotating magnet beneath the beaker, while a ceramic stir bar is not.
